passage:
I'm Reena, Zubin's neighbour. I was on the stairs when it happened, so I can only say what I saw.
It was eleven at night after his board exam. Zubin was sitting on the landing with his phone, eyes red from studying. He said, half to himself, "My gaming account gets locked in 30 minutes?" He tapped the link and started typing fast. I heard him mutter his password.
Two minutes later he went pale. An email said his password had been changed.
He didn't say much. He put his head on his knees. I guessed he felt stupid, but I don't know for sure.
I sat down next to him and said, "Anyone falls for that when they're this tired." Then his father came out, looked at the screen, and helped him reset his passwords and report the message. His father only said, "Good that you told us straight away."

qa.q: What did the message say would happen in 30 minutes?
qa.a: It said Zubin's gaming account would get locked in 30 minutes.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling with his head on his knees?
qa.a: He may have felt stupid and upset, though Reena could not know for sure; he had just lost control of his account.

qa.q: What helped after Zubin tapped the link?
qa.a: Telling his father straight away meant the passwords were reset and the message reported quickly, and no one shamed him for it.

qa.q: What would change if Zubin had seen the message the next morning, rested?
qa.a: Without exhaustion and the late-night rush, he might have paused, checked the account directly and noticed the fake link.

grounding: A neighbour watches a tired student tap a fake locked-account link late at night, and his father helps him recover without blame.

passage:
Wednesday. Jomon laughed when Mohit showed him a fake prize text. "Who even falls for these?"
Friday. After a double maths test and cricket practice, Jomon was half asleep on the bus when a text came: Your parcel could not be delivered. Update address within 1 hour or it will be returned. He was expecting new football boots from his uncle. He tapped, filled in his address, then his mother's card details for a redelivery fee of 25 rupees. Only on the stairs home did it hit him: the boots were coming by courier, not post.
He told his mother that night, pale and stammering. She didn't yell. She blocked the card within minutes.
Sunday. Jomon sat with Mohit, scrolling back through the text. "I was so sure I'd never fall for it," he said. "I was just tired."

qa.q: What was Jomon expecting from his uncle?
qa.a: He was expecting new football boots from his uncle.

qa.q: What did Jomon feel on the stairs home?
qa.a: It suddenly hit him that the text was fake, and he felt a rush of alarm and embarrassment.

qa.q: What did Jomon do right after realising?
qa.a: He told his mother that same night, and she blocked the card within minutes, which limited the damage.

qa.q: How might Mohit see things differently after Sunday?
qa.a: Mohit might see that even someone who laughed at scam texts can be caught when tired, and feel more careful himself.

grounding: A boy who once mocked scam texts taps a fake delivery link on a tired day, then tells his mother, who blocks the card that night.

passage:
I'm Chaitanya, and I got caught by the oldest trick there is, on the most tired night of my life.
It was 1 a.m., the night before my board practical. I'd been studying for hours. A message popped up: "Your game account will be deleted in 30 minutes due to suspicious activity. Verify now." With a link.
My account had two years of progress. I didn't think. I tapped the link and typed my email and password.
Five minutes later, my account was gone, and the email password was changed too.
I felt sick. I'm the one who laughs at my uncle for forwarding fake messages.
In the morning I told my friend Eshaan. He didn't laugh. He said, "Tired plus panic, that's exactly when they get people." He helped me reset everything from the official site, and I told my father, who helped me report it.
Now I have a rule: nothing urgent after midnight.

qa.q: What time was it when Chaitanya got the message?
qa.a: It was 1 a.m.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel after the account was taken?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt sick and embarrassed, especially after laughing at an uncle for forwarding fake messages.

qa.q: What helped Chaitanya recover?
qa.a: Eshaan helped reset everything from the official site, and Chaitanya told a parent who helped report it.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see what happened?
qa.a: Eshaan sees it as a normal trap that uses tiredness and panic, not as Chaitanya being foolish.

grounding: A teenager recalls tapping a phishing link under urgency on a tired night, showing that anyone can be caught.

passage:
School IT teacher's note, exam week, Thursday. From Hemant.
Baljeet, Class 11, came to the computer lab at lunch looking worried. Last night, while revising late, she got a text: "Your parcel delivery failed. Update address in 2 hours or it will be returned." She was expecting books for her exam, so she tapped the link, entered her address, and then her mother's card details for a "₹25 redelivery fee."
By morning she realised something was wrong. She said, "I'm so stupid. I know about phishing. We did it in class."
I told her that urgency and tiredness are exactly what these messages count on, and that even careful adults get caught.
We called her mother at work immediately. Her mother blocked the card through the bank's official app. We also reported the message on the cybercrime portal and forwarded it to the class as a real example, with Baljeet's permission.

qa.q: What did the text say about the parcel?
qa.a: Your parcel delivery failed. Update address in 2 hours or it will be returned.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when she came to the lab?
qa.a: Baljeet felt worried and ashamed, calling herself stupid because she had learned about phishing in class.

qa.q: What steps did the teacher take with Baljeet?
qa.a: The teacher reassured her anyone can be caught, called her mother immediately to block the card, reported the message, and shared it as a class example.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's classmates benefit from her example?
qa.a: They might feel more alert and less ashamed, seeing that a real classmate was caught on a tired day.

grounding: An IT teacher records a teenager tapping a fake delivery link under exam-week tiredness and urgency, and the quick steps that followed.

passage:
Wednesday, very late
I'm so annoyed with myself. At 11:40 tonight, after four hours of maths, a message came: "Congratulations Yash! You've won a new phone in the student lucky draw. Claim in 15 minutes!" It had my name. My actual name.
I was so tired and so curious that I tapped it and entered my email and password to "log in."
Then the page asked for a card number. That's when I woke up. I closed it. But they already had my email password.
I messaged Baljeet, who knows computers. She replied in two minutes: "Change your password NOW from the real site, and turn on two-step login. Then tell your dad." I did all of it. Dad was half asleep but he helped me check that nothing else was linked.
Baljeet said, "Don't feel stupid. They use your name so you'll trust it." I still feel stupid. But less.

qa.q: How many minutes did the message give Yash to claim the phone?
qa.a: Claim in 15 minutes.

qa.q: How does Yash feel at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Yash feels annoyed and a bit stupid, but less so after Baljeet's reassurance.

qa.q: What steps did Yash take after realising the mistake?
qa.a: Yash changed the password from the real site, turned on two-step login, and told Dad, who helped check everything.

qa.q: How does Baljeet see what happened to Yash?
qa.a: Baljeet sees it as a trick that uses Yash's name to build trust, not as Yash being stupid.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows tapping a prize link when tired and curious, and fixing it quickly with help.
